itineraries.title: The River, the Falls, the Redeemer - 11 Day Itinerary
editorial: Eleven days sounds generous until you remember the size of Brazil. This route is fast, flight-heavy and worth it if you want radically different versions of the country in one trip.
What if we had more time?
We'd slow everything down before adding destinations. Give the Amazon another night, Rio another day and leave more breathing room around flights.
On a return trip, we'd explore the northeast rather than adding yet another stop to this one.

days.title: Day 1 - Manaus
editorial: Land in Manaus and acclimatise to the heat.
It was brutally hot when we arrived, even before the jungle entered the itinerary. Eat local fish—Tambaqui de Banda was our introduction—and sleep early.
Manaus is the gateway, not merely a layover. The city exists because the Amazon is a transport network as much as a natural wonder.

days.title: Day 2 - Amazon
editorial: Head into the Amazon and see the Meeting of Waters, where the dark Rio Negro runs alongside the lighter Solimoes without immediately mixing.

The science is interesting—differences in temperature, density, velocity and chemistry—but the visual is what sticks. Two giant rivers sharing a boundary line in open water looks fake even when you are floating through it.

The environmental fragility was harder to ignore. Smoke hung over a rainforest that should be too humid to burn naturally, and extreme water temperatures had recently killed large numbers of river dolphins.

days.title: Day 3 - Amazon
editorial: Go deeper.

We spent the night sleeping in hammocks in the jungle after eating chicken and fish grilled over a campfire. There are trips where your hotel matters and trips where you wake up thinking, “What even is this life?” This was the latter.
One guide showed us how striking certain trees can carry sound kilometres through the forest—a reminder that humans had figured out communications infrastructure here long before telecom towers.

days.title: Day 4 - Amazon
editorial: Use the final jungle day to understand life along the river.
Families live kilometres apart on the banks, boats are the only practical transport and everyday supplies become expensive simply because moving goods through the Amazon is expensive.
Fishing, river transport and isolated settlements make the forest feel less like a tourist attraction and more like an inhabited world you have briefly been allowed into.

days.title: Day 5 - Rio de Janeiro
editorial: Fly to Rio and stay around Copacabana or Ipanema.
Our first impression of Copacabana was surprisingly familiar: seaside apartment blocks and urban density gave us South Mumbai vibes, only with mountains casually rising behind the beach.
Eat feijoada. We had an excellent bowl for around USD8 near Copacabana. Black beans, beef and pork—dense enough to reset your relationship with lunch.

days.title: Day 6 - Rio de Janeiro
editorial: Visit Christ the Redeemer and spend the rest of the day looking at Rio from as many angles as possible.
The statue itself is interesting; the setting is transcendent. Rio may be the most naturally scenic city we have visited: mountains, ocean, bays and islands all crammed into one urban frame.
Unlike some religious monuments, the atmosphere around Christ felt cheerful rather than solemn. Giant Jesus, selfie sticks, spectacular view. Everybody seemed fine with the arrangement.

days.title: Day 7 - Rio de Janeiro
editorial: Leave some unscheduled time for the beaches and city.
The Cathedral of Saint Sebastian surprised us. Its interior has the same calming effect we felt inside Hagia Sophia: faith aside, people behaving quietly together can make a building feel peaceful.
Rio's inequality is visible too, and parts of the city require more awareness than the postcard suggests. Enjoy the beauty without sleepwalking through it.

days.title: Day 8 - Foz do Iguacu
editorial: Fly to Foz do Iguacu and recover from the journey.
The town sits beside both Argentina and Paraguay, which is geographically delightful and logistically useful if you are extending the trip.
Foz itself felt polished and tourism-driven compared with Manaus, with prices to match.

days.title: Day 9 - Iguacu Falls
editorial: This is the second main event after the Amazon.
Take the falls seriously enough to get wet. Our boat ride through the rapids was short and exhilarating; the falls themselves were something else entirely.
I wrote in my notes that they were a spiritual experience, second only to the aurora borealis. Time has not improved that sentence, so we'll keep it.
Avoid overpaying for a “private tour” that is essentially a glorified transfer. We did and eventually got a refund.

days.title: Day 10 - Sao Paulo
editorial: Fly to Sao Paulo and use the evening for food.
Our flight was diverted because of bad weather, which killed dinner plans with friends and neatly summarised the downside of a domestic-flight-heavy itinerary.
Sao Paulo felt more liveable than touristy. Our neighbourhood was quiet on a Sunday night, but restaurants stayed busy late. We found good ramen, which is not what Brazil brochures lead with.

days.title: Day 11 - Sao Paulo
editorial: If museums are open, this is their day. Ours happened to be a Monday, which removed many of the obvious options.
We left Sao Paulo feeling it was a city we'd rather live in for a month than sightsee in for a day.

One final practical lesson came at the airport: international health and transit requirements can interact in unexpected ways. Check the current vaccination rules for Brazil and your onward destination before flying. Do not learn this at the check-in counter.
